text:
Recent work favors evaluating verifiable evidence and user outcomes separately. A [2024 analysis](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aaai.12182) argues explanations help decision-making when users can verify predictions. A [2025 recommendation-evaluation framework](https://beyondrecsys.github.io/2025/paper2.pdf) combines correctness, sufficiency, recency, uncertainty, usefulness, and actual interaction. Implication: a plausible history-based rationale is evidence of possible relevance, not proof of the ranker’s reasoning or the user’s willingness to choose.

For this task, a proposed audit rubric should distinguish explicit choice, tentative interest, explicit rejection, and unknown; separately label capability redundancy, documented specification conflicts, and recent-interest matches. Attach each label to an exact feedback span, timestamped interaction, or title/description passage. Similar purchases alone cannot establish ownership, redundancy, incompatibility, or unmet needs. Missing compatibility specifications should yield “unknown.” This rubric is a task-specific synthesis, not an established taxonomy. [AbstentionBench (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038) finds abstention unreliable across diverse unanswerable questions; prompting alone does not resolve uncertainty handling.

For the twenty-user audit, independently double-annotate examples using a fixed codebook, preserve disagreements, and adjudicate ambiguous cases. Report raw agreement plus a chance-corrected reliability measure, per-label counts, and abstention coverage; assess automated labels against held-out human annotations where feasible. Report user-level uncertainty intervals and category counts, treating repeated recommendations within a user as dependent. Five users per category support exploratory case analysis, not confident population claims. Do not infer unobserved diversity/conformity traits or convert tentative interest into acceptance.
